title: THE POWER OF INDOCTRINATION
mv: Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
mvp: “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.” Colossians 2:8
assignment: Mention two (2) personal lessons you have learned from this topic (5x2=10 marks).

b.x: The concept of indoctrination originally refers to education, i.e. instructing a person or people on the fundamentals of a belief or ideology, but later acquired the negative meaning of teaching someone to accept a set of beliefs without questioning them. The goal of the Christian faith is to liberate rather than enslave, and the approach to teaching it precludes force, coercion or manipulation. The power of indoctrination depends on what is being taught and how it is being taught. This lesson examines how indoctrination can be used for both good (discipleship in truth) and evil (deception and control).

False indoctrination leads people away from truth, enslaving them to lies, wrong ideologies, and traditions (Matthew 15:8-9). Interpreting the Bible from the place of mediocrity, half-truth and human philosophy will mislead. In Galatians 1:6-9, Paul warns of corrupt gospel messages. Indoctrination can lead to spiritual ruin if it is based on lies. For example, King Nebuchadnezzar developed an ‘indoctrination programme’ in Daniel Chapter 1, to reprogramme the minds of the Jewish youths. He changed their names, taught them Babylonian literature and gave them Babylonian food. However, Daniel resisted indoctrination that violated God’s truth (Daniel 1:8).

People can be subtly indoctrinated into deception through misinformation, disinformation, malinformation, gas lighting, social reinforcement, emotional appeals, repetition, etc., via platforms like social media. These channels exploit cognitive biases and present incomplete or skewed information, shaping individuals' perceptions and encouraging acceptance of false realities without obvious coercion (2 Corinthians 11:13-15).

God commands the passing on of truth from generation to generation (Deuteronomy 6:6-7). Bible doctrines contain some kingdom realities that the human mind and intelligence may not fully comprehend or explain. The response to such realities is simply faith and trust in God’s manifold wisdom (1 Corinthians 2:10-14; Ephesians 3:9-12).

To teach and disciple others appropriately in truth begins with approaching the Bible, God’s word, with an open mind, void of preconceived idea, notion or hidden motive (Psalm 119:18; Proverbs 2:6). It involves recognising that some portions of the Bible are written in coded languages that demands proper study and research to decipher (Luke 18:25; Hebrews 5:14). It entails submitting to the Holy Spirit to truly open our spiritual senses to discover His mind and not to affirm our own opinion (Isaiah 50:4-5; Ephesians 1:18). It is to be intentional in ensuring that our lives align with the truth of God's word (2 Timothy 3:14-17). A clear example of discipleship in truth through indoctrination is seen in Jesus' teaching His disciples and “opening their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures” (Luke 24:45). Jesus indoctrinated His disciples in truth-not by coercion, but by revelation and understanding.

To guard against false indoctrination, believers must be ready to test every teaching as well as the spirit in operation (1 John 4:1; Ephesians 4:14). We must grow up in the faith; learning, practicing and teaching the truth (Hebrews 6:1; Ephesians 4:15) and steering clear from false prophets and fake pastors/teachers whose belly has become their gods and who have questionable conducts (Matthew 7:15; Philippians 3:17-19).
Indoctrination is powerful, but the source and content matter (John 8:31-32).

i: Mention three ways to guard against false indoctrination.
